remarks: “In loans from CA one may also hear q for *q, eg qabīlitna ”“our tribe”“, ḥuquq ”“rights”“, muṯaqqafīn ”“educated people”“, or ḳ as in aḳall ”“less”“. In katal, yuktul”“beat; kill”“ *q has a k reflex, as well as in kinābil alhawn ”“mortar shells”“ (recorded in RA) . Notice that in the instance of katal, yuktul a back-formation of the devoiced g under the influence of voiceless t in the imperfect, i.e. regressive partial assimilation in *yugtul (pronounced[' yuktul ]), appears to plausibly account for the presence of voiceless k throughout the conjugation. ”

The interdentals (plain and emphatic) are currently in a state of variability with their stop counterparts. The origin of the variability in Amman is the contact between Jordanian dialects, which have interdentals, and Madanī Palestinian dialects, which do not. In the case of the plain interdentals, /ṯ/ and /ḏ/, many speakers (especially the male speakers) use them variably with /t/ and /d/. The emphatic interdental,/ḏ̣/, shows a considerably lower degree of variation with the stop variant /ḍ/ in the speech of the same speaker, i.e., the speakers tend to use either one or the other. The speakers who use the emphatic interdental are exclusively of Jordanian or Fallāḥī Palestinian origin and are most often male speakers, while those who use the stop counterpart can be from anywhere and of either sex (quote from al-Wer 2007a).

“BA is a mixed dialect, as it displays both Bedouin and urban features. Though the earlier studies record that early 20th century BA already had both urban and Bedouin features, the fact that even more Bedouin features appear in the dialect spoken today is no doubt the result of the massive migration of speakers of Bedouin varieties to Benghazi in the second half of the 20th century, where their varieties mixed with the pre‑existing, slightly more urban dialect of Benghazi. The mass influx of Bedouin forms on top of these earlier urban ones has also resulted in either a) a few features which are some sort of merged Bedouin/urban form, b) the coexistence of both forms simultaneously, or c) confusion as to which form is more correct. This mixed aspect appears throughout the dialect’s phonetic, syntactic, and morphological systems, as well as in the lexicon. Nevertheless, as P. MARÇAIS already pointed out, Benghazi Arabic, like nearly all dialects of Libya, is remarkably conservative (MARÇAIS 1977: ix)... Thus it may be said that the Arabic dialect of Benghazi is overall a Bedouin dialect, with some features from an older, slightly more urbanized variety. As a result of the intense migration of rural Bedouin from eastern Libya to Benghazi, BA has been influenced by a number of Bedouin features.” (Benkato 2014: 92-93, 95)

remarks: reflex for CA *ǧ is ǧ (I.P.A. [ʤ]), but the tip of the tongue is nearer to the alveolar ridge resulting in less of a resonance cavity created by the blade of the tongue. When directly preceding alveolar consonants n, I, t, d, y and r much of the friction in the release is lost, yielding a sound between [d] and [dy], and [d] with a lateral release when followed by I ... When /ǧ/ is realized intervocalically in allegro style, only minimal articulatory contact, if any, may be realized, the result being almost [y] with hardly any friction

remarks: Elderly (70+), Old (60-70) and some middle age speakers show consistent raising of short medial a in unstressed closed syllable before ā, in the pattern CaCCāC(v), as in: nižžār (carpenter), fillāḥ (peasant) and, surprisingly, ḥimmām (toilet, bathroom) and xirbāna (spoiled, broken). Other examples of this, outside of the aforementioned pattern is miʕnāt-a (hence, lit. her meaning). The examples suggest that a preceding /ḥ/ or /x/ does not always block the raising in this pattern.

remarks: Elderly (70+), Old (60-70) and some middle age speakers show consistent raising of short medial a in unstressed open syllable before ī.

In this pattern the conditioning seems to be consistent as shown in the preservation of a in ġarīb (strange), qalīl (a little), ṭawīl (long), xafīfa (light. F) and gaṛīḅa (near. F). Nevertheless, probably due to influence from BEI, in this pattern a is sometimes elided altogether, often in rather frequent adjectives such as mnīḥ (good) kbīr (big) and ktīr (a lot).

remarks: Elderly (70+), Old (60-70) and some middle age speakers show consistent raising of short medial a in stressed open syllable. The quality of the vowel seems to be sensitive to pharyngealization and labiality, thus, in environments combining labial and gutural consonants we find u: guṃar (moon), gufaṣ (cage). Raising is blocked in instances like saʕal (he asked), ṛagaṣ (he danced). In our data, so far, /h/, /ʕ/ and /x/ as C1 do not seem to systematically block the raising of a in CáCaC / CáCa patterns, while /ʔ/, /ḥ/, /ʕ/ as C2 do seem to systematically block the raising of a

remarks: “The speech of the Lebanese tribes appears to have been affected considerably by the surrounding sedentary dialects in respect of this feature. For the younger speakers the stress tends to fall on the second syllable: yišt'aġal (he works), etc., whilst amongst older speakers it can fall on the same syllable or on the first: y'ištaġal (he works), etc. The first type is clearly the more sedentary variety (Behnstedt 1997:142-143), and, as was noted above (5.6.2.6.1) the second is more typical of Bedouin dialects.” (Pickett 2005: 244).

remarks: Younes (2014:361-362) notes that: “Nous constatons que la présence d’une vélaire engendre une élévation assez centralisée tandis que dans un environnement plus neutre, la voyelle /a/ s’élèvera vers le /i/. Ceci est tout de même soumis à quelques exceptions puisque nous avons noté : dǝxīl « personne trouvant refuge », mǝdīn « ayant une dette (m.) » mǝsīr « chemin, trajet ». Tel que relevé, il semble que la présence d’une labiale dans un contexte emphatique tire la voyelle /a/ vers /u/ : ṭuẉīla « longue, haute ». Also he notes: ”De manière analogue à ce qui se passe dans les autres parlers nomades d’Orient, nous observons une inhibition systématique de l’imāla si C1 correspond à /ʾ/, /ʿ/, /h/, /ḥ/, /ġ/ ou /x/“.

remarks: Younes 2014:363 notes that in this case, the raising is blocked mainly when C1 is a guttural or when C2 is either l, r, or n, but with the exception of ḥ and ʕ, which seem to cause only partial raising to ə, while following labial consonants and the occurrence of m seem to render u instead of i: “En effet, pour ce schème, la règle implique que si C1 correspond à /ʾ/, /ʿ/, /h/, /ḥ/, /ġ/ ou /x/ ou alors si C2 correspond à /l/, /r/ ou /n/ même si dans ce dernier cas la distribution est aléatoire, l’élévation n’a pas lieu. Les pharyngales /ḥ/ et /ʿ/ pourraient avoir un traitement à part sur certains schèmes ce qui expliquerait les réalisations enregistrées. Pour ce qu’il en est de la laryngale /ʾ/, la coloration en /u/ de la voyelle est probablement le résultat de la bilabiale qui suit, en l’occurrence /m/”.

remarks: The voiceless velar stop *k presents three main variants: namely /k/, the affricate variant /č/ (tʃ and the postalveolar fricative /š/ (ʃ). Instances of /č/ are generally conditioned by the presence of a front vowel in the environment of *k, e.g. yimčin (maybe), činno (as if), haḏīč (that.SG.F), but not only, as examples such as čam (how much) or čānat (she was) show. As for the variant /š/, we assume it to result from assibilation of /č/, and it appears more frequently in middle age and young speakers than in old speakers.

Affrication of k to č is normally identified as one of the most salient features marking the “Bedouin” character of this community's variety. Variant š, although present in the data, is considered a mark of “urban Bedouins” that do not know how to speak “proper Bedouin”.

remarks: Elderly (70+), Old (60-70) and some middle age speakers show consistent raising of short medial a in unstressed closed syllable before ā, in the pattern CaCCāC(v), as in: nižžār (carpenter), fillāḥ (peasant) and, surprisingly, ḥimmām (toilet, bathroom) and xirbāna (spoiled, broken). Other examples of this, outside of the aforementioned pattern is miʕnāt-a (hence, lit. her meaning). The examples suggest that a preceding /ḥ/ or /x/ does not always block the raising in this pattern.

remarks: Elderly (70+), Old (60-70) and some middle age speakers show consistent raising of short medial a in unstressed open syllable before ī.

In this pattern the conditioning seems to be consistent as shown in the preservation of a in ġarīb (strange), qalīl (a little), ṭawīl (long), xafīfa (light. F) and gaṛīḅa (near. F). Nevertheless, probably due to influence from BEI, in this pattern a is sometimes elided altogether, often in rather frequent adjectives such as mnīḥ (good) kbīr (big) and ktīr (a lot).

remarks: Elderly (70+), Old (60-70) and some middle age speakers show consistent raising of short medial a in stressed open syllable. The quality of the vowel seems to be sensitive to pharyngealization and labiality, thus, in environments combining labial and gutural consonants we find u: guṃar (moon), gufaṣ (cage). Raising is blocked in instances like saʕal (he asked), ṛagaṣ (he danced). In our data, so far, /h/, /ʕ/ and /x/ as C1 do not seem to systematically block the raising of a in CáCaC / CáCa patterns, while /ʔ/, /ḥ/, /ʕ/ as C2 do seem to systematically block the raising of a

remarks: “The speech of the Lebanese tribes appears to have been affected considerably by the surrounding sedentary dialects in respect of this feature. For the younger speakers the stress tends to fall on the second syllable: yišt'aġal (he works), etc., whilst amongst older speakers it can fall on the same syllable or on the first: y'ištaġal (he works), etc. The first type is clearly the more sedentary variety (Behnstedt 1997:142-143), and, as was noted above (5.6.2.6.1) the second is more typical of Bedouin dialects.” (Pickett 2005: 244).

In katal, yuktul”“beat; kill”“ *q has a k reflex, as well as in kinābil alhawn ”“mortar shells”“ (recorded in RA) . Notice that in the instance of katal, yuktul a back-formation of the devoiced g under the influence of voiceless t in the imperfect, i.e. regressive partial assimilation in *yugtul (pronounced[' yuktul ]), appears to plausibly account for the presence of voiceless k throughout the conjugation. ”

“Indivative with b- prefix was introduced in the last 20/30 years. B- indicative occurs in the following contexts, arranged in terms of increasing frequency: after coordinate u dependent on verb wudd/widd, subordinate cl. n- we, t- maa (neg.) first sing, third person. (Some of the contexts are not mutually exclusive, e.g., n- we occurs in subordinate clauses, after u and, etc., though we did not check the combined effect of these variable factors on the distribution of b-.) What this says is that b- is least likely to occur after u ”and“ and in a position dependent on a verb or on wudd ”want“; it is a little more common (though not much) in subordinate clauses (adverbial and conditionals constitute the largest sets of tokens here) and before the person prefix n- we; it occurs occasionally, though still in less than 60 percent of the tokens, after negative maa and with first person subjects and the subject markers t- (second person, third feminine, cf.2.1). By far its most extensive occurrence is with a third person subject in main, non-negative clause.” (Owens 1984:214)

remarks: “The speech of the Lebanese tribes appears to have been affected considerably by the surrounding sedentary dialects in respect of this feature. For the younger speakers the stress tends to fall on the second syllable: yišt'aġal (he works), etc., whilst amongst older speakers it can fall on the same syllable or on the first: y'ištaġal (he works), etc. The first type is clearly the more sedentary variety (Behnstedt 1997:142-143), and, as was noted above (5.6.2.6.1) the second is more typical of Bedouin dialects.” (Pickett 2005: 244).

remarks: reflex for CA *ǧ is ǧ (I.P.A. [ʤ]), but the tip of the tongue is nearer to the alveolar ridge resulting in less of a resonance cavity created by the blade of the tongue. When directly preceding alveolar consonants n, I, t, d, y and r much of the friction in the release is lost, yielding a sound between [d] and [dy], and [d] with a lateral release when followed by I ... When /ǧ/ is realized intervocalically in allegro style, only minimal articulatory contact, if any, may be realized, the result being almost [y] with hardly any friction

remarks: “In loans from CA one may also hear q for *q, eg qabīlitna ”“our tribe”“, ḥuquq ”“rights”“, muṯaqqafīn ”“educated people”“, or ḳ as in aḳall ”“less”“. In katal, yuktul”“beat; kill”“ *q has a k reflex, as well as in kinābil alhawn ”“mortar shells”“ (recorded in RA) . Notice that in the instance of katal, yuktul a back-formation of the devoiced g under the influence of voiceless t in the imperfect, i.e. regressive partial assimilation in *yugtul (pronounced[' yuktul ]), appears to plausibly account for the presence of voiceless k throughout the conjugation. ”

remarks: Form IV has a factitive value. “La valeur générale de la forme IV, comme en arabe standard, est factitive” (Younes 2013: 49)

Form IV seems to be in the process of being replaced by form II due to the pressure of sedentary dialects: “Toutefois, sous la pression des parlers sédentaires, la fonction factitive est aussi largement assurée par le schème C1aC2C2aC3: waggaf-ywaggif «faire cesser», sammaʿ-ysammiʿ «faire entendre». On voit en synchronie qu’il existe une concurrence entre les formes IV et II dans des verbes tels que ʾabʿad ~ baʿʿad «éloigner», ʾaṭʿam ~ tạ ʿʿam «nourrir» mais également entre les formes IV et I dans ʾasga ~ siga «abreuver, irriguer»” (Younes 2013: 49).
